units.text:
Quality
 Quality means fitness for use.
   • There are two general aspects of fitness for use: quality of design and quality of
    conformance.

 Quality is inversely proportional to variability.
   • A few years ago, one of the automobile companies in the United States performed a
    comparative study of a transmission that was manufactured in a domestic plant and by a
    Japanese supplier.
   • An analysis of warranty claims and repair costs indicated that there was a striking
     difference between the two sources of production, with the Japanese-produced
     transmission having much lower costs.

units.text:
Quality Engineering terminology


 Every product possesses a number of elements that jointly describe what the
    user or consumer thinks of as quality. These parameters are often called quality
     characteristics. Sometimes these are called critical-to-quality (CTQ)
     characteristics. B may be of several types:
      Physical: length, weight, voltage, viscosity
     Sensory: taste, appearance, color
    Time Orientation: reliability, durability, serviceability
 Quality engineering is the set of operational, managerial, and engineering
     activities that a company uses to ensure that the quality characteristics of a
    product are at the nominal or required levels and that the variability around
    these desired levels is minimum.
 Other terminologies: statistical methods; variability; attributes or variables;
     specifications; nominal or target value; upper specification limit (USL); lower
     specification limit (LSL); over-the-wall; nonconforming products; nonconformity;
     defective; defects; concurrent engineering.

units.text:
History of Quality Control and
Improvement
Frederick W. Taylor introduced some principles of scientific management as mass
   production industries began to develop prior to 1900
Frank Gilbreth and others extended this concept to the study of motion and work
   design
In 1924, Walter A. Shewhart of the Bell Telephone Laboratories developed the
    statistical control chart concept, which is often considered the formal beginning of
    statistical quality control. Toward the end of the 1920s, Harold F. Dodge and Harry
   G. Romig, both of Bell Telephone Laboratories, developed statistically based
   acceptance sampling as an alternative to 100% inspection. By the middle of the
   1930s, statistical quality-control methods were in wide use at Western Electric, the
   manufacturing arm of the Bell System.
The American Society for Quality Control was formed in 1946. This organization
   promotes the use of quality improvement techniques for all types of products and
   services
The 1950s and 1960s saw the emergence of reliability engineering
In the 1950s, designed experiments for product and process improvement were
    first introduced in the United States.
                                        ME3327E QUALITY, RELIABILITY AND

The 7 Core Pillars of QMS (ISO 9001)

ISO 9001 standard frameworks are anchored in seven fundamental
Quality Management Principles (QMPs) configured for organizational
cohesion:

 1.  Customer Focus: Meeting needs and striving to exceed expectations.
 2.  Leadership: Creating unity of purpose and corporate direction.
 3.  Engagement of People: Empowering competent staff at all tiers.
 4.  Process Approach: Managing activities as interrelated, logical
    workflows.
 5.  Improvement: Maintaining an ongoing focal commitment to
     optimization.
 6.  Evidence-based Decisions: Choosing paths based on systemic data
     analysis.
 7.  Relationship Management: Nurturing mutual value with critical
     partners.

units.text:
Strategic Value Propositions

Implementing QMS principles is not a compliance checklist; it dictates
commercial survival and high-velocity scaling:

   Risk Mitigation & Resilience
   Standardizing key pathways radically minimizes downstream product
    failure, scrap rates, regulatory litigation, and catastrophic public recalls.

   Cost Reductions & Profitability
   Directly optimizes internal resource allocation, removing redundant
   actions, reducing process variations, and conserving operational
   runway.
  Brand Equity & Customer Trust
    Delivering uniform outputs repeatedly matches expectations, creating
    stable organic retention rates and justifying premium pricing structures.

units.text:
The Road to Operational Excellence


        Align & Design:
        Strategic Setup: Translate the seven QMPs into explicit, top-tier corporate
         objectives, establishing clear metrics of success and process benchmarks.


           Process Mapping:
             Practical Execution: Embed standard checkpoints inside production
             workflows. Establish visible, accessible document hierarchies and
            feedback chains.

          Engage & Train:
            Sustain Engagement: Decentralize standard checks. Train teams to
             run root-cause analysis locally, eliminating functional communication
                silos.

        Excel & Evolve:
       Peak Standards: Run data audits regularly. Execute continuous
        improvement loops (Kaizen, DMAIC) to transition from standard control into
         predictive Quality 4.0.
                                    ME3327E QUALITY, RELIABILITY AND

Dimensions of Quality





                                       ME3327E QUALITY, RELIABILITY AND

Key Components of Quality Management

        Quality Planning

       • Establish quality objectives and determine the necessary processes,
          resources, and timelines to meet them.

        Quality Assurance

       • Implement systematic, preventive measures and maintain
        documented procedures to ensure that processes consistently
         produce compliant outcomes.

        Quality Control

       • Monitor outputs using inspections, testing, and measurement to
          detect deviations from specifications.

        Quality Improvement

       • Continuously enhance processes by identifying inefficiencies and
         removing root causes of defects or failures.

Acceptance sampling

Acceptance sampling, defined as the inspection and classification of a
sample of units selected at random from a larger batch or lot and the
ultimate decision about disposition of the lot, usually occurs at two
points: incoming raw materials or components, or final production.
